entry: Genre of broadcast program in which contestants compete for prizes. The host typically directs the show, explaining its rules and narrating where necessary. The genre became popular in the United States in the 1950s, becoming a regular feature of daytime television. In a traditional game show, prizes can be won within a single episode through objective completion of tasks rather than fan or contestant votes. Contestants, sometimes as part of a team, answer trivia questions or solve puzzles for prizes such as cash, trips and goods and services. [[Jeopardy!]] is the only trivia-based game show that allows unlimited consecutive appearances, as long as contestants keep winning. Game shows differ from [[Reality television|reality television]] competitions, which typically involve judging or voting, and shows such as [[American Idol]] do not count as game shows for that reason.

Branch of applied mathematics that models interactions between multiple agents as games of strategy. Game theory describes, predicts and evaluates choices, often to maximize payoffs for one or more players. It is applied in the natural, formal and social sciences, including [[Biology|biology]], [[Computer science|computer science]], [[Economics|economics]], law, logic and political science. Its genesis lies in the 1944 book *Theory of Games and Economic Behavior* by mathematicians [[John von Neumann]] and Oskar Morgenstern. Initially used to describe firms, markets and consumers, it has since been applied to animal behavior, international relations and voting systems. In 1994 the Nobel Prize in economics went to John Nash, John Harsanyi and Reinhard Selten for their work in the field.

Traditional ensemble music of the Javanese, Sundanese and Balinese peoples of [[Indonesia]]. Gamelan is made up predominantly of percussive instruments, most commonly metallophones played with mallets and a set of hand-drums called kendang, which keep the beat. Other instruments include [[Xylophone|xylophones]], [[Bamboo|bamboo]] flutes and a bowed string instrument called the rebab. Vocalists may also be featured. Gamelan is traditionally performed to accompany religious [[Ritual|rituals]], ceremonies, dance, theater and wayang puppet theater, and it remains commonly played at official cultural, corporate and government events. Its popularity has declined slightly since modern popular music arrived in Indonesia. In 2014 gamelan traditions were recognized as part of Indonesia's National Intangible Cultural Heritage, and on December 15, 2021, gamelan was inscribed on the UNESCO Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity.

Haploid stage in the life cycle of plants and algae. The gametophyte is one of the two alternating multicellular phases in plant life cycles, developing from a haploid spore and bearing sex organs that produce gametes. Gametes fuse in fertilization to form a diploid zygote, which develops into the [[Sporophyte|sporophyte]] phase; the sporophyte produces haploid spores by [[Meiosis|meiosis]] that germinate into new gametophytes. In [[Bryophyte|bryophytes]] such as mosses, liverworts and hornworts, the gametophyte is the most visible and longest-lived stage and is nutritionally independent, while the sporophyte depends on it. In most [[Fern|ferns]], the gametophyte is a photosynthetic, free-living structure called a prothallus, which maintains the sporophyte during its early development. As land plants evolved reproduction by seeds, the female gametophyte became smaller and more dependent on the sporophyte.

Versatile two-parameter family of continuous probability distributions. The [[Exponential distribution|exponential]], Erlang and [[Chi-squared distribution|chi-squared]] distributions are special cases. In econometrics it is used to model waiting times, and in [[Bayesian statistics]] it serves as a conjugate prior for inverse scale parameters. If the shape parameter is a positive integer, the distribution is an Erlang distribution, the sum of that many independent exponentially distributed variables.

Most common extension of the factorial function to [[Complex number|complex numbers]]. Denoted by Γ, it is defined for all complex numbers except non-positive integers, and satisfies Γ(n) = (n−1)! for every positive integer n. [[Daniel Bernoulli]] first studied it. For complex numbers with positive real part it is defined by a convergent improper integral, and analytic continuation extends it to a meromorphic function over the complex plane. Because the gamma function has no zeros, its reciprocal is an entire function. It is not the only extension of the factorial, but it is the most popular and useful, and it appears as a factor in probability distribution functions and formulas in probability, statistics, [[Analytic number theory]] and [[Combinatorics|combinatorics]].

Penetrating form of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]]. Gamma rays arise from high-energy interactions, such as the radioactive decay of atomic nuclei or astronomical events like solar flares. The French chemist and physicist Paul Villard discovered gamma radiation in 1900 while studying radiation from radium. In 1903 [[Ernest Rutherford]] named it gamma rays for its relatively strong penetration of matter. Gamma rays from radioactive decay have energies from ten kiloelectronvolts (keV) to 10 megaelectronvolts (MeV), and their energy spectrum can identify decaying radionuclides. Gamma rays are ionizing radiation that can cause DNA mutations and cancer, and their penetration requires shielding of dense materials such as [[Lead]] or [[Concrete]].

Extremely energetic explosion in a distant galaxy, releasing a brief flash of gamma rays. Gamma-ray bursts are the brightest and most powerful class of explosion in the universe, second only to the Big Bang as the most energetic and luminous phenomena known. A burst can last from a few milliseconds to several hours and is followed by a longer-lived afterglow at X-ray, ultraviolet, optical, infrared or radio wavelengths. Most are thought to be released during a supernova as a high-mass star implodes to form a [[Neutron star|neutron star]] or [[Black hole|black hole]], while short bursts come from mergers of binary neutron stars. A burst in the [[Milky Way]] pointed at Earth would likely cause a mass extinction, and some researchers have hypothesized that the [[Late Ordovician mass extinction]] resulted from one.

Wizard and protagonist in J. R. R. Tolkien's novels *The Hobbit* and *The Lord of the Rings*. One of the Istari, he works mostly by encouraging and persuading and is associated with fire. In *The Hobbit* he helps a company of dwarves retake the Lonely Mountain from the dragon Smaug. In *The Lord of the Rings* he leads the Fellowship of the Ring, is killed fighting a Balrog, and returns as Gandalf the White. Scholars have likened him to the Norse god [[Odin]]. Ian McKellen played him in Peter Jackson's films.

Hindu deity identified by his elephant head and four arms. Ganesha is revered as the remover of obstacles and bringer of good luck, the patron of arts and sciences, and the deity of logic, intellect and wisdom. As the god of beginnings, he is honored at the start of rites and ceremonies, and he is invoked during writing sessions as a patron of letters. Hindu texts identify him as the son of [[Parvati]] and [[Shiva]], though he is a pan-Hindu god found across traditions. He is mentioned in Hindu texts between the 1st century BCE and 2nd century CE, and his devotion extends to Jains and Buddhists. Eight famous Ganesha temples in [[Maharashtra]] are known as the Ashtavinayak.

Group of individuals who engage in illegal and violent behavior. Members usually glorify an aggressive and antisocial lifestyle, and many gangs are made up of lifelong friends or relatives. Gangs emerged in U.S. cities by the middle of the 19th century, and [[Chicago]] alone had over 1,000 gangs in the 1920s. By 2011 gang presence in the United States was estimated at 1.4 million active members in about 33,000 gangs. In El Salvador, the rival gangs [[MS-13]] and Barrio 18 have dominated the criminal landscape, with approximately 60,000 active members around 2012. In the 2020s gangs in [[Haiti]] expanded their control of Port-au-Prince, and in 2025 the [[United Nations Security Council]] authorized the Gang Suppression Force to support Haitian security forces.

Form of [[Group sex|group sex]] in which one person is the central focus of several participants, usually more than three. The term generally refers to a woman as the focus, and a "reverse gang bang" has one man and many women. It has become associated with the [[Pornographic film|pornography industry]], where it usually describes a staged event. *Bukkake*, a type of gang bang that originated in Japan, centers on the person being ejaculated upon by multiple male participants. Three people engaged in sex is normally called a [[Threesome|threesome]].

Cluster of neuron cell bodies in the peripheral nervous system. Ganglia are made up primarily of cell bodies and dendritic structures, and they serve as relay points between the peripheral and [[Central nervous system|central]] nervous systems. Among vertebrates, dorsal root ganglia contain the cell bodies of sensory neurons, cranial nerve ganglia contain those of cranial nerve neurons, and autonomic ganglia contain those of autonomic nerves. In the brain, the [[Basal ganglia|basal ganglia]] are a group of nuclei interconnected with the [[Cerebral cortex|cerebral cortex]], thalamus and [[Brainstem|brainstem]], though the Terminologia Anatomica recommends the term basal nuclei. A pseudoganglion is a thickening of a nerve that resembles a ganglion but has only nerve fibers and no cell bodies.

K-pop song by South Korean singer Psy. Released on July 15, 2012, as the lead single from his sixth studio album, *Psy 6 (Six Rules), Part 1*, "Gangnam Style" satirizes the nouveau riche lifestyle associated with Seoul's Gangnam district. The music video went viral in August 2012, and on December 21, 2012, it became the first [[YouTube]] video to reach a billion views. The song peaked at number two on the Billboard Hot 100, the highest position for a South Korean artist at the time, and topped the music charts of more than 30 countries. In 2013 U.S. President [[Barack Obama]] cited its success as an example of the Korean Wave of culture.

Type of tissue death caused by a lack of blood supply. Symptoms may include a change in skin color to red or black, numbness, pain, swelling and coolness, most often in the feet and hands. Risk factors include [[Diabetes|diabetes]], peripheral arterial disease, [[Smoking|smoking]], major trauma, alcoholism, HIV/AIDS and frostbite. Infection can also cause gangrene, which may present with fever or [[Sepsis|sepsis]]. Types include dry, wet, gas and internal gangrene, as well as necrotizing fasciitis. Dry gangrene results from chronic ischemia without infection, while wet gangrene is infected and carries a poorer prognosis because of sepsis risk. Treatment may involve surgery to remove dead tissue, including [[Amputation|amputation]], antibiotics for infection, and bypass surgery or angioplasty for the underlying cause. In some cases hyperbaric oxygen therapy may be useful.

Natural satellite of [[Jupiter]] and the largest moon in the [[Solar System]]. Ganymede is composed of silicate rock and water in roughly equal proportions, with an iron-rich liquid metallic core. It orbits Jupiter in roughly seven days. It is the only natural satellite in the Solar System known to generate its own magnetic field, probably through convection within its core. Its internal ocean potentially contains more water than all of Earth's oceans combined. The surface has lighter regions crossed by grooves and ridges and darker regions saturated with impact craters. Simon Marius and [[Galileo Galilei]] both observed it in 1610, and Marius named it after a Trojan prince who became cupbearer to the gods. The [[Voyager 1]] and [[Voyager 2]] probes refined measurements of its size, and the Galileo spacecraft discovered its underground ocean and magnetic field.

Walled, roofed structure with a door for storing vehicles. A residential garage may be attached to a home, with an entry door into the house, or be a separate detached outbuilding. It protects a vehicle from precipitation and, if it has a locking door, from theft and vandalism. Most garages also serve as workshops, and some are used for storage or entertainment. Some garage doors open and close electrically at the press of a [[Remote control|remote control]]. Uninsulated attached garages can reach freezing temperatures in northern climates, and poor insulation allows [[Heat transfer|heat transfer]] into adjoining living areas. The word garage, introduced to English in 1902, comes from the French word *garer*, meaning shelter.

Biblical paradise described in Genesis 2–3 and Ezekiel 28 and 31. Also called the Garden of God, it is described in Genesis as the source of four rivers, including the Tigris and Euphrates. Proposed locations include the head of the [[Persian Gulf]], southern [[Mesopotamia]] and Armenia. In Genesis, God places the first man, [[Adam]], in the garden, where one tree, the tree of knowledge of good and evil, is forbidden. After the couple eats the forbidden fruit, they are expelled.

Genus of flowering plants in the [[Rubiaceae|coffee family]]. Native to the tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, Asia, [[Madagascar]], the Pacific Islands and Australia, the genus was named by [[Carl Linnaeus]] and John Ellis after the Scottish naturalist Alexander Garden. Most species grow as shrubs or small trees, and many have large, showy white, cream or pale yellow flowers with a strong scent that is often more noticeable at night. *Gardenia jasminoides*, the type species, is grown as a houseplant and demands high humidity and bright, indirect light. Its fruit is used in [[Traditional Chinese medicine|traditional Chinese medicine]]. As of July 2022, *Plants of the World Online* recognized 128 species in the genus.

Practice of growing plants for their vegetables, fruits, flowers, herbs or ornamental purposes. Gardens serve many purposes, including aesthetically pleasing areas, medicines, cosmetics, dyes, foods, poisons, wildlife habitats and saleable goods. Gardening ranges in scale from the 800-hectare Versailles gardens to container gardens grown indoors. Practices respond to cultural moments: victory gardens were grown during World War II, and biodiversity-focused gardening, such as native plant gardening, has developed in reaction to biodiversity loss. Gardening is difficult to distinguish from [[Agriculture|farming]], though farming prioritizes saleable goods, while gardening often prioritizes aesthetics and leisure on a smaller scale. People garden for therapeutic, health, educational, cultural and environmental benefits.

Welsh former professional footballer who played as a right winger. He played most notably for Tottenham Hotspur and [[Madrid|Real Madrid]], and he was a five-time [[UEFA Champions League]] winner. He had 111 caps for Wales and scored 41 goals, making him Wales' most capped player and top goalscorer, and he was named Welsh Footballer of the Year a record six times. He joined Los Angeles FC in [[Major League Soccer]] in July 2022, winning an MLS Cup.

Species of bulbous flowering plant in the genus *Allium*. Garlic (*Allium sativum*) is native to Central Asia and northeastern Iran and has naturalized in Mediterranean Europe and China. Its close relatives include the [[Onion|onion]], shallot, [[Leek|leek]] and chives. It has been used for thousands of years as a seasoning and traditional medicine, and clinical evidence indicates that consuming it has health benefits. Sulfur compounds give garlic its pungent odor and flavor; allicin is most responsible for the hot taste of raw garlic, and cooking removes it. China was the largest producer in 2024, accounting for 73% of the world's supply, according to the [[United Nations]] FAOSTAT database.

Group of silicate minerals used since the Bronze Age as gemstones and abrasives. Garnet species share similar physical and crystallographic properties but differ widely in chemical composition, falling into two main solid solution series. Garnets are most often associated with [[Metamorphic rock|metamorphic rock]], though they occasionally occur in volcanic rocks. They occur in nearly every color, with reddish shades most common, and blue garnets are the rarest. Garnets have a [[Mohs scale|Mohs]] hardness of about 6.0 to 7.5, and the harder almandine is used for abrasives.

Russian [[Chess|chess]] grandmaster, political activist and writer. He was World Chess Champion from 1985 to 2000 and became the youngest undisputed champion in 1985, at age 22, by defeating Anatoly Karpov. His peak FIDE rating of 2851, achieved in 1999, was the highest recorded until [[Magnus Carlsen]] surpassed it in 2013. In 1997 he became the first world champion to lose a match to a computer under standard time controls, when he was defeated by the [[IBM]] supercomputer Deep Blue. He retired from regular competitive chess in 2005 and turned to writing and politics, opposing the policies of [[Vladimir Putin]] and leaving Russia in 2013 out of fear of persecution. He chaired the Human Rights Foundation from 2011 to 2024.

Common name for snakes of the genus *Thamnophis* in the family Colubridae. Garter snakes are small to medium-sized snakes native to North and Central America, ranging from central [[Canada]] south to [[Costa Rica]]. About 37 species and 52 subspecies are recognized, though taxonomists disagree on classification. They have large round eyes, a slender build, keeled scales and longitudinal stripes that may or may not include spots. They live near water and eat mostly amphibians, along with fish and earthworms. Garter snakes may retain toxins from their amphibian prey in the liver, making them among the few snakes that can be both venomous and poisonous. Mass emergences from communal [[Hibernation|hibernation]] in spring facilitate mating.
